Volume 04 · Chapter 10

Time-series and panel data basics

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v04-c09

By the endPrepare longitudinal data and identify dependence and aggregation pitfalls.

The calendar and the population are part of the variable

Capability: prepare longitudinal data with correct entity–time keys and lags, and identify dependence, selection and aggregation pitfalls. Prerequisite: prediction and validation with economic timing, together with the table/key methods of Chapter 4 and covariance calculations from Volume 3. All tables and stochastic laws here are original synthetic teaching constructions, not observations of actual firms or current economic conditions.

A firm appears in January and March but not February. The previous row is January; the previous month is February. Treating the two as interchangeable creates a false monthly change. A second problem arises when the March sample contains new firms and excludes closed ones: its mean can fall even if every retained complete-case firm's sales rose. Neither error is repaired by fitting a more elaborate regression.

A time series follows a defined variable across ordered times. A panel follows identified entities across times. In a monthly firm panel, write yit for firm i's value in calendar month t. The key is (firm identifier, month), with exactly one row at the declared grain. Repeated cross-sections survey different units at each date; they do not become a panel because they contain the same variables. Stable identifiers require care around mergers, reorganizations or reassignment: an unchanged label need not imply an unchanged economic unit.

Record what each date means: observation instant, interval covered, publication date or extraction vintage. Monthly sales cover an interval; month-end inventory describes an instant. A release published in April may refer to March, and later revisions may change it. The calendar lag below concerns the reference period. Whether that lagged value was available at a forecast origin remains the separate information-time check from Chapter 9.

Calendar-correct lags, differences and gaps

For regular monthly periods, the first lag is Lyit = yi,t−1. A first difference is Δyit = yit − yi,t−1. A proportional growth rate is git = yit/yi,t−1 − 1 when the denominator is nonzero; its usual positive-level interpretation requires positive levels. If a needed value is absent, the lag, difference and growth calculation are unavailable. Do not turn an absent value into zero or substitute a different date. If the denominator is a genuine zero, growth is undefined, even though a level difference may be meaningful.

Represent a month by an integer m = 12 × year + (month number − 1). December 2023 then precedes January 2024 by exactly one. For each row, look up the key (i, m − 1) in a unique-key table. Sorting is useful for display, but a row shift is a monthly lag only when the entity is unchanged and the reference months are consecutive. A 12-month lag means the same month of the prior year, not twelve earlier observed rows. Daily trading lags require a specified trading calendar; the previous trading session and previous calendar day differ.

A missing row, an explicitly missing value, a structural absence and a measured zero carry different information. A firm not yet operating has no active firm-month observation; an active firm failing to report has an unknown value. A confirmed zero-sales month remains an observed value. A filled calendar grid exposes these states but does not supply missing economics. Preserve a reason or status field. After a join, check that no duplicate key multiplied a record; dropping duplicates arbitrarily may discard genuinely different establishments or vintages that should instead change the grain.

The official Stata panel-declaration reference explains within-panel time ordering, gaps and a specified time step. Its concepts are useful even though this chapter implements the lookup directly in standard-library Python and requires no Stata installation.

Deflate with a price measure matched to the question

Let Nit be a current-dollar amount and Pt a suitable price index with base period b equal to 100. The corresponding constant-base-dollar amount is Rit = 100Nit/Pt. To see the meaning without an index-number theorem, suppose all firms sell one homogeneous good whose base price is 1 USD and current price is Pt/100 USD per unit. Then Nit = (Pt/100)qit, so Rit = qit × 1 USD per unit. In our examples this deliberately simple assumption makes deflation exact.

In applications, a household consumption index, an output-price index and an investment-goods index target different baskets. Currency conversion is another operation, not a substitute for choosing prices and quantities consistently. Use the index's level, not its inflation percentage, and match period, geography, coverage and vintage. An index merely rebased to 100 changes the numerical constant-dollar unit; it does not by itself supply new price information.

Rₜ/Rₛ = (Nₜ/Nₛ)/(Pₜ/Pₛ), so 1 + greal = (1 + gnominal)/(1 + inflation).

Subtracting inflation from nominal growth is an approximation, not this exact identity. Negative or zero index levels make the proposed deflator invalid; negative nominal amounts may be legitimate signed flows but require a separate interpretation of percentage growth. With multiple products and changing relative prices, official real aggregates can use chain-weighted index methods; their published components need not add like our single-good constant-base amounts. Follow the series' stated construction.

BEA's explanation of PCE prices and quantities describes appropriate detailed deflators and chain-weighted aggregation. It supports the need to identify the price measure; our one-good teaching index is not a model of the full PCE system.

Worked example 1: missing reports, changing membership and real sales

The window is January–March 2024. All firms sell the one good just defined; the synthetic output-price indexes are 100, 110 and 120. A and B operate throughout. C begins in February. D ceases before March, with the roster confirming no March operation. B's February sales report is missing while it remains active. These facts come from a separate roster; they cannot be deduced from the observed sales rows alone.

Monthly sales in USD; real amounts use January 2024 prices
FirmMonthNominal salesPrice indexReal salesPrevious calendar month's real sales
AJanuary100100100Outside window
AFebruary121110110100
AMarch144120120110
BJanuary200100200Outside window
BFebruaryUnreported110Unknown200
BMarch216120180Unknown
CJanuaryNot operating100Not an active observationOutside window
CFebruary330110300Not operating
CMarch360120300300
DJanuary400100400Outside window
DFebruary330110300400
DMarchNot operating120Not an active observation300

For A, February real growth is 110/100 − 1 = 10%, while March growth is 120/110 − 1 = 1/11 ≈ 9.0909%. For B, the previous observed real sale before March is 200 in January; 180/200 − 1 = −10% is a two-month change. Calling it a monthly change would invent the February information. C's March growth is zero; its February growth from a nonexistent active observation is unavailable.

The means across observed reports are 700/3 in January, 710/3 in February and 600/3 = 200 in March, in constant-January USD. February uses A, C and D: (110 + 300 + 300)/3 = 710/3 ≈ 236.667. Each mean uses three reports, but the reporting firms differ across months. January-to-March observed-mean growth is 200/(700/3) − 1 = −1/7 ≈ −14.2857%.

Two different fixed cohorts tell different stories. Firms observed at both endpoints are A and B: mean real sales are 150 at each endpoint, so their change is zero. A is the only firm with all three active monthly reports: the complete-window mean rises from 100 to 120, or 20%. Requiring a balanced complete panel therefore changes the target and selects against missing reports as well as entry and exit. Neither selected cohort measures the whole evolving population automatically.

For the total sales of this explicitly closed roster, nonoperating firm-months can contribute zero because no sales occur outside their documented operating intervals. Endpoint totals are 700 and 600. The change decomposes as continuing firms' change (120 − 100) + (180 − 200) = 0, plus entrant C's 300, minus exiting D's 400: −100. February's total for all active firms remains unknown because B is unreported. The observed subtotal 710 must not be labeled a complete total. Using zero for a documented nonoperating sales flow is a target-specific accounting decision, not a license to zero-fill unknown records or stock variables.

Panel balance, survivorship and dependence

A panel balanced on a chosen set of dates contains the same entities with the required observations at every date. An unbalanced panel does not. “Balanced” describes a data structure; it does not certify random sampling or comparability. Keep the roster and inclusion flow: eligible entities, observed entities, missing outcomes, entries, exits and exclusions by period. Report the count behind every mean. A larger observed average may reflect a different population rather than improvement for a typical continuing entity.

Survivorship selection occurs when analysis uses future survival or continued reporting to choose earlier records. A fund-performance table containing only currently operating funds can omit earlier failed funds; a worker panel restricted to those still employed can omit departures. The selected average is valid for its stated selected group, but does not identify the original group's performance without assumptions about missing members. Requiring “complete data” can itself use future information. A weighting or imputation correction requires a defensible model for observation and the target; balance alone supplies none.

Panel rows are often dependent within an entity and across entities exposed to the same period shock. In Yit = αi + Ct + uit, fixed αi describes persistent firm differences, Ct is a shared time shock and uit is an individual disturbance. If Ct and the individual disturbances have mean zero, Ct is independent of those disturbances, and different firms' uit are uncorrelated, two different firms in the same month share covariance Var(Ct). Counting N × T rows as that many independent observations ignores this structure. Appropriate inference depends on the sampling and shock model; this chapter diagnoses the issue rather than prescribing one universal standard error.

Changing frequency requires changing the operation

Choose aggregation by economic meaning, not by a default spreadsheet function
ObjectExamplePossible quarter constructionRequired qualification
Flow over disjoint intervalsMonthly sales or units deliveredSum the three complete monthly amountsNo overlapping intervals; consistent coverage and units
Stock at an instantMonth-end inventoryUse quarter-end stock for a quarter-end targetAn average stock requires observations/assumptions covering time, not a sum
Ratio of accumulated flowsDefective units / delivered unitsSum numerators and denominators separately, then divideThis weights monthly rates by their denominator exposures
Compounding returnMonthly total investment returnMultiply gross returns: ∏(1+rt) − 1Consistent reinvestment and cash-flow convention
Published annualized level or rateQuarterly output at an annual rate; annualized quarterly growthUndo the specified annualization before the needed calculationA rate label and a period total are different units

A quarter-end stock is not necessarily the most recent available stock if the quarter-end reading is missing. A monthly flow is not the average of a few sampled days unless a measurement design justifies that conversion. An interval crossing a month boundary requires dated underlying events or an explicit allocation assumption; assigning the whole interval to its ending month changes the object. Seasonal adjustment also changes a series' construction and can be revised; record whether the input is adjusted before comparing frequencies or reconstructing real-time data.

For nonnegative denominator exposures dt with positive total, a pooled rate is Σnt/Σdt = Σ[dt/Σds](nt/dt) over positive denominators. A zero denominator does not define a monthly rate; zero numerator and denominator contribute zero exposure to the pooled ratio. A positive numerator with zero exposure signals an inconsistent definition. An unweighted average of monthly percentages instead gives every month equal weight, which can be a legitimate different target if stated.

A quarterly flow reported as an annualized level of 480 USD under the convention “four times this quarter's flow” corresponds to 120 USD for that quarter. By contrast, an annualized quarterly growth rate a satisfies 1 + a = (1 + g)4 when compounding is the convention. For positive gross growth, g = (1 + a)1/4 − 1; dividing a by four is only an approximation. These operations must not be mixed.

BEA's quarterly growth annualization explanation specifies compounding a quarterly rate for four quarters. The chapter's amounts and percentages are original examples; no current GDP release is used.

Worked example 2: one quarter, four different calculations

A separate synthetic workshop has the following monthly records. Sales concern the same single good with January price 1 USD. Deliveries and defective deliveries are disjoint monthly counts; each defective delivery is included in its month's delivered count. Investment returns describe a separate fully reinvested account with no external deposits or withdrawals.

MonthNominal sales, USDPrice indexReal sales, January USDEnd inventory, unitsDefects / deliveriesAccount return
January120100120102 / 1010%
February220110200163 / 30−10%
March36012030096 / 2020%

Quarter nominal sales are 700 USD. Deflate each monthly flow at its matched monthly price and then sum: 120 + 200 + 300 = 620 January USD. Deflating the 700 total by the unweighted mean index 110 instead gives 7000/11 ≈ 636.364, which is different. The aggregate deflator consistent with this particular real total is 100(700/620) = 3500/31 ≈ 112.9032. It reflects the sales pattern; it is not simply the arithmetic mean of the three monthly indexes. This one-good result does not assert that official multi-good chain indexes can always be added.

Quarter-end inventory is 9 units, not 10 + 16 + 9 = 35. The average of the three observed endpoint stocks is 35/3, but a quarter's time-average stock is not identified by those three endpoints alone: different within-month inventory paths can share them. Quarterly defective-delivery share is (2 + 3 + 6)/(10 + 30 + 20) = 11/60 ≈ 18.3333%. Averaging the monthly shares (20% + 10% + 30%)/3 gives 20%, an equally weighted monthly-rate summary rather than the fraction of this quarter's delivered units that were defective.

The account's quarterly gross return is (11/10)(9/10)(6/5) = 297/250, hence return 47/250 = 18.8%. Adding the monthly returns gives 20% and ignores compounding. A 100 USD initial account balance becomes 110, then 99, then 118.80 USD. If there were external cash flows, these balances alone would not identify the same reinvested return measure.

Stationarity describes a law, not a flat-looking line

A realized time plot is one path of random variables {Yt}. A process is weakly stationary, also called covariance stationary, if it has finite second moments, E[Yt] = μ independent of t, and Cov(Yt, Yt−h) = γ(h) depending only on the lag h, not on the calendar date t. Variance γ(0) is consequently constant. If γ(0) > 0, the autocorrelation is ρ(h) = γ(h)/γ(0); for a constant zero-variance process this ratio is undefined. Weak stationarity constrains first and second moments, not every feature of the joint distribution.

It does not require successive observations to be equal or independent. Consider independent identically distributed shocks εt with values −2 and 2, each with probability 1/2, indexed over all integer times. Thus Eεt = 0 and Var(εt) = 4. Define

Yₜ = 10 + εₜ + (1/2)εₜ₋₁.

The mean is 10. Independence makes the two shocks' covariance zero, so Var(Yt) = 4 + (1/4)4 = 5. Adjacent values share exactly one shock: Cov(Yt,Yt−1) = Cov((1/2)εt−1,εt−1) = 2. At lag |h| ≥ 2 they share no shocks, and their covariance is zero. Thus γ(0) = 5, γ(±1) = 2 and γ(h) = 0 elsewhere, with ρ(1) = 2/5. Every quantity is independent of t: this is stationary dependent data. The construction is a moving-average process of order one, or MA(1); it is not the same operation as averaging observed monthly values for presentation.

For n consecutive observations of any weakly stationary process, summing all variances and covariances gives

Var(Ȳₙ) = [nγ(0) + 2Σh=1n−1(n−h)γ(h)]/n².

There are n diagonal variance terms and n − h pairs at each positive lag h, counted twice in the full double sum. For the MA(1) above, this becomes [5n + 4(n − 1)]/n² = (9n − 4)/n². For n = 4 it is 2, whereas treating the observations as independent gives 5/4. The additional observations provide information, but not at the independent-observation rate assumed by that naive calculation.

Mikusheva's MIT notes on stationarity, lag operators and covariance provide a route to fuller time-series theory. The finite-shock construction and covariance derivation above establish the particular law used here without appealing to an unexplained large-sample theorem.

Trends, random walks and transformations

Using the same iid shocks, the process Tt = 3t + εt has constant variance 4 but mean 3t, so it is not weakly stationary. Subtracting its known deterministic trend leaves εt, which is stationary. A fixed calendar seasonal mean, such as a different expected sales level each December, also violates a constant unconditional mean. Estimating and removing a trend or seasonal pattern is a modeling choice; doing so with future data can additionally violate a forecasting information boundary.

For a different law, take W0 = 0 and Wt = Σs=1tεs for t ≥ 1. This random walk has E[Wt] = 0 but Var(Wt) = 4t. For s ≤ t, Wt = Ws plus independent later shocks, so Cov(Ws,Wt) = 4s. Its changing variance violates stationarity despite its constant mean. Differencing gives ΔWt = εt, a stationary sequence. Adding deterministic drift d per period gives mean dt in levels and mean d in the stationary increments.

Detrending and differencing answer different questions. For Tt = 3t + εt, differences are 3 + εt − εt−1, with variance 8 and adjacent covariance −4. Differencing a deterministic-trend-plus-independent-noise model has introduced negative serial dependence; subtracting the known trend leaves independent shocks. Conversely, subtracting a deterministic line from the random walk does not eliminate its growing variance. Differencing, logging or seasonal adjustment is not a universal stationarity repair.

Stationarity alone also does not guarantee that one long sample average learns the population mean. Let Yt = C + ut, where the common C has mean zero and variance τ² > 0, and iid ut have mean zero and variance σ², independently of C. This process is weakly stationary: γ(0) = τ² + σ² and γ(h) = τ² for nonzero h. Yet Var(Ȳn) = τ² + σ²/n does not approach zero. More directly, the averaged u term has mean-square size σ²/n and converges to zero in mean square, so Ȳn converges in mean square to C. A single path retains its nondegenerate common component instead of converging to the population mean zero. Assumptions permitting time averages to recover population quantities must be established in addition to stationary moments.

Hyndman and Athanasopoulos's stationarity and differencing discussion connects trend, seasonality and differencing to forecasting. Our examples distinguish laws by their proved moments; a plotted path alone cannot establish those moments for all dates.

Diagnose dependence without pretending to prove stationarity

For a complete equally spaced sequence y1,…,yn, one common sample autocorrelation convention is

r̂(h) = [Σt=h+1n(yₜ−ȳ)(yₜ₋ₕ−ȳ)] / [Σt=1n(yₜ−ȳ)²], 0 ≤ h < n.

The same full-sample mean and denominator are used at every lag. Software using a different normalization may give different finite-sample values. A constant sample makes the denominator zero. With gaps, pairing must follow dates; silently compressing the records changes the meaning of h. Sample autocorrelations are diagnostics estimated from one path, not known population γ(h) or a proof of independence.

Inspect time plots, period coverage, within-entity paths, subgroup composition, rolling summaries and lagged plots. Investigate abrupt changes in definitions, prices or coverage before interpreting a break economically. Persistent autocorrelation can reflect a stationary dependent law, a deterministic trend, an accumulating shock, a shared component or aggregation. A short stable-looking segment can occur under a changing law. Tests and richer models require explicit alternatives, sampling assumptions and finite-sample caution; full time-series and panel inference belongs to the later econometrics volume.

Offline longitudinal-data laboratory

Download the standard-library Python program, synthetic roster, monthly records and price inputs, and README into one folder. Run python3 v04-c10-panel.py. The report shows a complete entity–month status grid, exact deflated values and calendar lags, cohort and observed-sample summaries, the quarter calculations and exact MA/random-walk moment targets. It does not write or repair the original file.

The input fixes a short monthly window and explicit operating intervals. Its supported units remain nominal USD per month and constant-January-2024 USD; the window must include January 2024 with index 100. The program rejects different unit labels or base normalization rather than silently reinterpreting them. Observed rows must lie inside an entity's operating interval; every month has one positive price-index value. Duplicate keys, unknown entities, bad dates, missing index months and inconsistent counts are rejected. Missing active sales rows remain unknown. The program distinguishes them from nonoperating periods and counts the denominator of each summary. As a small local teaching tool, it does not infer a merger history, validate an externally supplied roster's truth, or estimate stationary laws from the synthetic panel.

def month_number(text):
    year, month = map(int, text.split("-"))
    if not 1 <= month <= 12:
        raise ValueError("month must be 01 through 12")
    return 12 * year + month - 1

sales = {("B", month_number("2024-01")): 200,
         ("B", month_number("2024-03")): 216}
key = ("B", month_number("2024-03") - 1)
print(sales.get(key))  # None: February is absent, not zero

This small illustration assumes strings already have the intended year-month form; the download adds strict text and range validation. Dictionary get returns None for an absent key by default. The computation retains the calendar distinction even when input rows are shuffled. Real sales use exact fractions from integer inputs, so output such as "710/3" means an exact rational result, not a decimal estimate of statistical precision.

Laboratory deliverable: reconcile both examples, shuffle the observations to verify unchanged results, remove B's March report to expose the changed coverage, and deliberately insert a duplicate key to verify refusal. Submit the active/observed counts, exact endpoint and complete-window comparisons, and one sentence explaining each aggregation operation. A satisfactory report preserves unknown values, states the chosen population and makes no claim that these constructed records prove stationarity or causality.

Exercises

  1. Calendar gaps. Firm K reports 80 in December 2023 and 100 in February 2024; firm J reports 7 in January 2024 and 8 in February. All are positive same-unit monthly values. Give each firm's February monthly lag, difference and growth when defined. Give K's observed two-month growth. Explain why an ordinary shift of rows, even after sorting by firm and month, needs an additional calendar check.
  2. Choose the panel target. Using example 1, compute January and March means for observed reports, for firms reported at both endpoints, and for firms reported in every month. Give all three percentage changes. Decompose the whole-roster total change into continuing, entering and exiting contributions. Explain why B's February omission cannot be filled like C's January nonoperation for the stated total-sales target.
  3. Deflation and rebasing. For A in example 1, compute January-to-March nominal growth, price inflation and real growth, and verify the exact gross-growth identity. Rebase the index so February equals 100; calculate the three new index levels and A's new constant-base sales. Explain which growth conclusions remain unchanged. Reconcile the correctly deflated quarter sales and implicit aggregate deflator in example 2.
  4. Aggregation transfer. A different quarter has monthly defects/deliveries 1/5, 0/15 and 4/20; endpoint inventories 8, 12 and 7 units; and fully reinvested account returns 5%, 0% and −5%. Find the pooled defect share, equally weighted monthly defect rate, quarter-end inventory and quarter return. A separate quarterly flow is published at 480 USD per year under four-times-quarter annualization: find the quarter amount. Can the time-average inventory or exact monthly allocation of a weekly flow spanning two months be recovered from these summaries alone?
  5. Stationary dependence. For Yt = 10 + εt + εt−1/2 with iid shocks ±2, derive its mean, variance, lag-one and lag-two covariance. Compute the exact variance and standard error of the average of four consecutive observations; compare with treating them as independent. State why positive autocorrelation does not refute weak stationarity.
  6. Trend versus random walk. With the same iid shocks, compare Tt = 3t + εt and Wt = Σs=1tεs. Give each mean and variance, Var(W5) and Cov(W2,W5). Derive the variance and adjacent covariance of each first-difference process. Does subtracting a known linear trend make both level processes stationary?
  7. A short path is limited evidence. For equally spaced observations (0, 1, 0, −1, 0), compute the stated sample autocorrelations at lags 1 and 2. A report says “lag-one correlation is zero, so observations are independent and stationary.” Assess that claim. State how missing dates and a constant sample would alter the computation.
  8. Shared shocks in panels. At one month, Yi = αi + C + ui for ten firms with fixed αi. C has mean zero and variance 9; independent ui have mean zero and variance 4, and are independent of C. Compute each outcome variance, covariance across two firms and the variance of the ten-firm average around its fixed mean. Compare with an independence calculation. Explain what a longitudinal analyst should document before selecting a variance estimator or using a complete-case panel.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. K's February monthly lag is unknown because January is absent; monthly difference and growth are therefore unavailable. Its observed December-to-February growth is 100/80 − 1 = 1/4 = 25%, covering two months. J's February lag is 7, difference is 1 and growth is 1/7 ≈ 14.2857%. Within-firm sorting does not insert absent calendar months. A shift must check both entity equality and a one-month gap; an ungrouped shift can additionally import another firm's observation. Month ordinals make December-to-January a one-month transition without confusing month numbers with dates.

  2. Observed-report means are 700/3 and 200, giving −1/7 ≈ −14.2857%. Endpoint-reported firms A and B have means (100+200)/2 = 150 and (120+180)/2 = 150, giving zero. The all-month complete group contains only A, with means 100 and 120, giving 20%. Whole-roster endpoint totals fall by 100: continuing firms contribute +20−20 = 0, C's entry adds 300 and D's exit removes 400. C is documented as nonoperating in January, and this specific sales-flow total assigns no sales outside operation. B is active in February with an unknown report; zero would assert an unobserved economic outcome and bias a claimed complete total. February observed subtotal 710 over three reports is therefore incomplete for four active firms.

  3. A's nominal growth is 144/100−1 = 44%; inflation is 120/100−1 = 20%; real growth is (144/120)/(100/100)−1 = 20%. Thus 1.44/1.20 = 1.20, whereas subtracting percentages gives the inaccurate 24%. The February-base price index is P′t = 100Pt/110: (1000/11,100,1200/11). New real amounts are 100N/P′ = (11/10)(100N/P), so A's values become 110,121,132 February-price USD. Every same-firm real growth ratio stays unchanged. Example 2 gives 100(120/100 + 220/110 + 360/120) = 620 January USD; its aggregate deflator is 100(700)/620 = 3500/31. The unweighted index average produces 7000/11, not 620.

  4. Pooled defects are 5 out of 40 deliveries: 1/8 = 12.5%. Monthly rates are 1/5,0,1/5, whose equally weighted mean is 2/15 ≈ 13.3333%. Quarter-end inventory is 7 units. The return is (21/20)(1)(19/20)−1 = −1/400 = −0.25%; a 100 USD starting balance ends at 99.75 USD, despite the monthly percentage sum being zero. The annualized flow level 480 corresponds to 120 USD in the quarter. Three endpoint stocks do not identify the time-average path. A weekly flow straddling months needs dated underlying transactions or a disclosed within-week allocation assumption; a total and endpoint date alone do not identify its monthly split.

  5. Shock mean is zero and variance is 4. Hence mean(Y) = 10, variance = 4 + (1/4)4 = 5, lag-one covariance = (1/2)4 = 2 and lag-two covariance = 0. Expanding the four-term average gives variance [4(5)+2(3)(2)]/16 = 32/16 = 2, so standard error is √2 ≈ 1.414214 outcome units. An independence calculation gives variance 5/4 and SE √5/2 ≈ 1.118034. Lag-one autocorrelation 2/5 is constant over time; weak stationarity permits it. Independence would instead require, among other things, zero covariance when second moments exist.

  6. T has mean 3t and variance 4; W has mean zero and variance 4t. Neither has stationary moments. Var(W5) = 20 and Cov(W2,W5) = Var(ε1+ε2) = 8. ΔTt = 3+εt−εt−1 has variance 8 and adjacent covariance −4 because the shared shock has opposite signs. ΔWt = εt has variance 4 and adjacent covariance zero. Both difference processes have constant mean and lag-dependent covariance. Subtracting the known 3t trend from T leaves stationary iid shocks. Subtracting any deterministic line from W changes its mean but leaves variance 4t; it cannot make the random-walk levels weakly stationary.

  7. The sample mean is zero and denominator is 1+1 = 2. Lag-one products are all zero, so r̂(1) = 0. At lag two the products are 0, −1 and 0, giving r̂(2) = −1/2. A sample estimate of zero at one lag proves neither all-lag zero covariance nor independence. Even population zero covariance at every nonzero lag would not imply independence without stronger assumptions. These five realized values cannot establish invariance of a generating law's moments at all dates. With missing dates, match observations h calendar periods apart and disclose the chosen missing-data estimator; do not compress time silently. A constant sample has zero denominator, so the stated sample correlation is undefined.

  8. Each firm has variance 9+4 = 13; two different firms share covariance 9. The average minus its fixed mean is C + (1/10)Σui, with variance 9+4/10 = 47/5 = 9.4. Treating ten outcomes as independent yields 13/10 = 1.3, substantially too small under this stipulated law. More firms do not average away the common month shock. A satisfactory documentation answer identifies entity and time keys, the sampling/observation mechanism, time and cross-entity shock dependence, the inference target, availability/vintage and the reasons for missing reports and entry/exit. Selecting only complete cases changes the population and can condition on future survival or reporting. Appropriate uncertainty and missingness methods require assumptions for those mechanisms; no particular estimator is justified by row count alone.

Teach-back and delayed check

Teach-back: explain to an analyst why the previous row can be the wrong lag, why a balanced panel can answer the wrong population question, and why quarter sales, quarter-end inventory, delivery ratios and returns require different aggregation. Then construct a stationary process with dependent observations and a nonstationary process with constant mean.

Delayed check, after 48 hours: a firm reports nominal sales 90 at price index 100 in December and 121 at index 110 in February, with January unreported. Calculate both real amounts and the observed change; state whether monthly growth is known. For iid mean-zero variance-1 shocks, give the variance and lag-one covariance of Zt = εt − εt−1.

Delayed-check answer

Real sales are 90 and 110 base-price USD, a level increase of 20 and an observed two-month growth of 110/90−1 = 2/9 ≈ 22.2222%. February monthly growth is unknown because January is unreported. Z has variance 2 and lag-one covariance −1; nonoverlapping shocks give zero covariance for |h| ≥ 2. Its mean and lag covariances do not depend on calendar time, so it is weakly stationary despite negative serial dependence.

Next: computational reliability and numerical audits develops systematic ways to detect wrong units, broken identities and fragile numerical results. Later econometrics adds estimation and inference for time and panel dependence, structural breaks, missingness and richer price-index construction.

Sources and further study

  • Stata — xtset: Declare data to be panel data — Primary software-author explanation of within-panel calendar ordering, time steps, missing dates and panel balance. Chapter implements concepts with original standard-library Python.
  • U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis — How are personal consumption expenditures prices and quantities derived? — Method source for appropriate detailed price-index deflation and chain-weighted aggregation; original one-good example separately derives exact period-specific deflation.
  • U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis — Why does BEA publish percent changes in quarterly series at annual rates? — Quarterly growth annualization through four-quarter compounding; distinguish growth-rate annualization from annualized flow-level units.
  • Anna Mikusheva, MIT OpenCourseWare — Lecture Notes 1: Stationarity, Lag Operator, ARMA, and Covariance Structure — Further-study route for covariance stationarity, lag operators and moving-average covariance structure; chapter gives original finite-shock proofs and numerical laws.
  • Rob J Hyndman and George Athanasopoulos — Forecasting: Principles and Practice, 3rd ed., Stationarity and differencing — Author-hosted further study connecting trends, seasonal differences and transformations to forecasting; original moment calculations establish the particular laws in this chapter.
